stem: When can you deny access to a safe deposit box?
options: During hazardous conditions such as a fire, flood, or pandemic
When complying with a court order or valid search warrant
When rental fees are unpaid or the lease is violated

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 10

flashcard.front: When can you deny access to a safe deposit box?
flashcard.back: Unsafe conditions (fire, flood, pandemic); court orders or valid search warrants; unpaid rent or a lease violation; reasonable suspicion of illicit or fraudulent activity

keyFact: Deny SDB access: hazards, court order/search warrant, unpaid rent or lease violation, suspected fraud

stem: Which of these is an effective restrictive indorsement?
why: "For Deposit" means the funds must be collected by a bank. A restriction like "Pay A only" does not prevent further negotiation; later holders can ignore it.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 21

flashcard.front: What are some examples of effective restrictive endorsements?
flashcard.back: "For Deposit" works: the funds must be collected by a bank. "Pay A only" doesn't stop further negotiation.

keyFact: Effective restrictive indorsement: "For Deposit" ("Pay A only" can be ignored)

stem: Who is typically liable for a forged payor signature on a check?
options: The person who presented the check
why: Under the "Final Payment Rule" the payor bank bears the loss, unless customer negligence substantially contributed or the customer failed to promptly report the forgery.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 23

flashcard.front: Who is typically liable for a forged payor signature on a check?
flashcard.back: The payor bank (Final Payment Rule), unless the customer's negligence contributed or they didn't report it promptly

keyFact: Forged drawer (payor) signature: payor bank bears the loss (Final Payment Rule)

stem: What types of negotiable instruments are included in Article 3 of the UCC?
options: Drafts (like checks) and notes (like promissory notes and CDs)
Controllable electronic records and digital assets
why: Article 3 covers negotiable instruments: drafts (a written order to pay, like checks) and notes (a written promise to pay, like promissory notes and CDs). Wires are 4A, secured transactions are 9, and electronic records are 12.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 17

flashcard.front: What types of negotiable instruments are included in Article 3 of the UCC?
flashcard.back: Drafts (written orders to pay, e.g. checks) and notes (written promises to pay, e.g. promissory notes, CDs)

keyFact: UCC Article 3: negotiable instruments (drafts and notes)

stem: When is it OK for a bank officer to act as a notary on a banking-related transaction?
options: Taking the acknowledgment of a party to a document executed to or by the bank, when the notary isn't a party to it
Notarizing a loan document the notary signed on behalf of the bank
Notarizing the notary's own loan with the bank
Never; bank personnel can't notarize anything related to the bank
why: Bank personnel who are notaries may take acknowledgments of parties to instruments executed to or by the bank, administer oaths to other bank personnel, and protest negotiable instruments held for collection.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 5

flashcard.front: When is it OK for a bank officer to act as a notary on a banking-related transaction?
flashcard.back: Taking acknowledgments of parties to instruments to/by the bank, administering oaths to bank personnel, protesting instruments held for collection, as long as the notary isn't a party

stem: When is it NOT OK for a bank officer to act as a notary on a banking-related transaction?
options: When the notary is a party to the instrument, individually or as the bank's representative
When the document is executed to or by the bank
When administering an oath to another bank employee
When protesting a negotiable instrument held for collection
why: It's unlawful for the notary to take the acknowledgment if they're a party to that instrument, whether individually or representing the bank. The notary must be an impartial third party.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 6

flashcard.front: When is it NOT OK for a bank officer to act as a notary on a banking-related transaction?
flashcard.back: When the notary is a party to the instrument, individually or as the bank's representative

keyFact: Bank notary: not OK if the notary is a party to the instrument (even for the bank)

stem: If you have a collateral sale, what are things that you must consider?
For a small estate transfer by affidavit, the aggregate deposits in the deceased's single-ownership accounts must be
why: The account must be in a sole individual's name with no P.O.D. beneficiary, and known heirs sign a sworn affidavit.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 8

keyFact: Small estate affidavit: $50,000 or less, single-owner accounts, no P.O.D.

stem: Which of these CAN an authorized signer (who isn't the owner) do on an account?
why: An authorized signer is a limited agent for transactions only. Unlike a power of attorney, they can't close, change beneficiaries, or pledge.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 8

keyFact: Authorized signer: deposits and withdrawals only

stem: Notice of an adverse claim to a deposit account requires the bank to hold the funds only when
options: Backed by a court order served on the depositor or an acceptable indemnity bond
The claimant sends a written letter
The claimant is a family member
why: Notice of an adverse claim alone isn't enough to freeze an account.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 6

keyFact: Adverse claim to deposits: hold only with a court order or indemnity bond

stem: A bank may enter into a deposit agreement directly with a minor, and a payment to the minor with a receipt signed by the minor discharges the bank.
why: The minor must be the sole and absolute owner of the account.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 5

stem: A standard Power of Attorney automatically grants access to the principal's safe deposit box.
why: Not unless the POA is specifically named and authorized on the box's lease agreement.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 10

keyFact: POA and safe deposit box: no access unless named on the lease

stem: Safe deposit box access requires dual control, meaning
options: The renter's key and the bank's master key used together
Two forms of ID from the renter

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 9

keyFact: SDB dual control: renter's key + bank's master key

stem: A lessee's written authorization for someone's post-death access to their safe deposit box is revoked by divorce unless it's re-executed.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 11

stem: When safe deposit rent is unpaid, after how many days of default does the bank send the 30-day notice by certified mail?
why: After 60 days' default, a 30-day notice goes by certified mail with the amount due and the opening date.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 14

keyFact: SDB unpaid rent: 60 days' default, then 30-day certified notice

stem: When a safe deposit box is drilled for nonpayment, it must be witnessed by
options: Two persons, one of them an officer
why: An inventory is made under oath, and the contents go into a secure package held by the lessor.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 14

keyFact: Drilling a box: 2 witnesses, one an officer; inventory under oath

stem: After a box is drilled, if no demand is made, how long before the lessor can advertise and sell the contents at public auction?

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 14

keyFact: Drilled box contents: sell at auction after 1 year

stem: If the surplus from a safe deposit box sale goes unclaimed, after how long is it presumed abandoned and turned over to the State Treasurer?

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 14

keyFact: Unclaimed SDB sale surplus: escheats after 5 years

stem: After a garnishment summons on a safe deposit box, if no court order directing entry is served within how many days is the box unsealed?
why: On service of the summons the lessor must immediately seal the box and deny access except as the court orders.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 15

keyFact: SDB garnishment: seal at once; unseal if no court order within 30 days

stem: A safe deposit box may be rented under a trade name regularly used in a valid business, if it's fully disclosed to the bank.
why: Otherwise, renting under an assumed name is prohibited.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 12

stem: A draft (like a check) commonly involves three parties. Which is the drawee?

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 17

keyFact: Draft parties: drawer (writes), payee (receives), drawee (bank holding funds)

stem: A note (like a promissory note or CD) involves which two parties?

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 18

keyFact: Note parties: maker (promises to pay) and payee

stem: Adding the words "Not Negotiable" makes a check non-negotiable.
why: It works on a promissory note, but this language does not make checks non-negotiable.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 19

keyFact: "Not Negotiable": works on notes, not on checks

stem: An instrument payable to bearer is negotiated by transfer of possession alone.
why: Instruments payable to an identified person need transfer of possession and indorsement.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 19

stem: A genuine check is made to a payee, but someone forges the payee's indorsement. Who bears the loss?
why: The depositary bank breached the presentment warranty of being "entitled to enforce," so the payor bank charges the loss back to it.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 23

keyFact: Forged indorsement: depositary bank bears the loss

stem: A completely counterfeit check with no genuine signature is paid. Who is liable?
why: The depositary bank only warrants it has no knowledge of a forged signature, so it didn't breach its warranty.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 24

keyFact: Counterfeit check: payor bank liable

stem: A genuine check's amount is altered (the drawer's signature is real). Who is liable?
why: Transfer and presentment warranties both include a strict-liability promise that the check hasn't been materially altered.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 24

keyFact: Material alteration: depositary bank liable

stem: Which UCC article governs funds transfers (wire transfers)?

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 16

keyFact: UCC articles: 3 instruments, 4 deposits & collections, 4A wires, 9 secured transactions, 12 electronic records

stem: To shift liability for an unauthorized wire to the customer, the bank must have
options: Offered and used a commercially reasonable security procedure, accepted the wire in good faith, and followed the procedure
Called the customer before every wire
why: Otherwise banks are generally strictly liable for unauthorized wires under Article 4A.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 25

keyFact: Wire fraud loss shift: commercially reasonable security, good faith, procedure followed

stem: UETA (electronic transactions) is mandatory for all parties to a transaction.
why: It only applies if both parties agreed to do business electronically. Best practice is clear, express consent up front.

source.ref: Bank Operations Law deck, handout page 27
